items.title: Artificial intelligence methods for morphological analysis and diagnosis of bacterial and fungal leaf diseases
items.abstract: Abstract Bacterial and fungal leaf diseases frequently produce overlapping visual symptoms, complicating automated diagnosis and limiting the transferability of models across crops and field conditions. This review systematically evaluates artificial intelligence methods for the morphology-based detection and differentiation of these diseases. Following a PRISMA-based selection process, 95 records published between 2017 and 2026 were identified, of which 59 eligible studies were included. The survey covers the morphological characteristics that distinguish bacterial and fungal diseases, traditional image processing and machine learning approaches, deep learning and generative AI techniques, and publicly available datasets. It also critically compares the performance, advantages, and limitations of existing diagnostic approaches. The findings indicate that deep learning dominates the literature, particularly in fungal disease detection, whereas research on bacterial diseases and generative AI applications remains comparatively limited. Although convolutional and transfer-learning models generally demonstrated strong classification performance, comparisons across studies were constrained by differences in datasets, evaluation protocols, and performance metrics. The principal barriers to practical adoption include morphological overlap between infections, class imbalance, and scarcity of expert-annotated images of bacterial and early-stage diseases, reliance on controlled-background datasets, limited external validation, model complexity, and insufficient interpretability. Future research should prioritize pathogen-balanced multicrop field datasets, standardized reporting and cross-dataset evaluation, multimodal fusion of RGB images with spectral and environmental data, domain adaptation, validated generative augmentation, explainable models, and lightweight edge deployment. By connecting lesion morphology with methodological and dataset evidence, this review provides a structured roadmap for developing robust, interpretable, and field-ready plant disease diagnosis systems.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence- Powered Smart Safety Cap for Farm Workers Using Artificial Intelligence, IoT and Wearable Sensors: A Review
items.abstract: Farm workers operating in sugarcane fields, forests, tea plantations, and other areas with thick vegetation may encounter hazardous animals and insects that are difficult to notice before approaching them. Conventional precautions, including sticks, torches, protective footwear, and visual observation, offer limited capability for identifying concealed threats in advance. Delays in communication and access to medical assistance can further increase the risks associated with such incidents. Recent progress in Artificial Intelligence (AI), computer vision, thermal imaging, edge computing, Global Positioning System (GPS) technology, and the Internet of Things (IoT) provides opportunities to develop wearable systems for improved agricultural safety. This paper presents a focused narrative review of research relevant to an AI-enabled safety cap, covering animal recognition, snake detection, thermal-based wildlife monitoring, edge deployment, and IoT- supported alert systems. The reviewed approaches are discussed across three areas: sensing methods, including visible-light cameras, thermal sensors, and supplementary positioning or motion sensors; deep-learning techniques, including YOLO -based detectors, transformer architectures, lightweight models, and object tracking; and system designs combining local processing, offline data handling, and cloud connectivity. Published results indicate that some animal and snake detection models achieve approximately 92–98% on selected evaluation metrics, while one thermal wildlife detection approach reports 89.1% mAP50 with approximately 1.45 million parameters. Certain lightweight YOLOv8 models have also demonstrated processing rates of around 52–65 frames per second on Jetson -class hardware, although performance may vary across devices and experimental settings. Despite these advances, much of the existing research relies on fixed cameras, aerial platforms, or controlled datasets. Limitations include restricted species coverage, insufficiently documented datasets partitioning, and limited evaluation under real agricultural conditions. The reviewed evidence does not establish the field performance of an integrated, multi-camera, head-worn safety device incorporating behaviour analysis, battery endurance assessment, and emergency alert testing. To address these gaps, this paper outlines a conceptual worker-to-cloud architecture combining visual and thermal sensing, edge-based inference, multi modal warnings, optional GPS-enabled SOS communication, and systematic field evaluation. The review also identifies research priorities for developing a practical and reliable wearable safety solution for agricultural workers.

items.title: Artificial intelligence-assisted physiologically based pharmacokinetic modeling and large-scale machine learning analysis of tumor delivery of nanoparticles in mice
items.abstract: Nanomedicine is a promising strategy for cancer therapy. However, the low delivery efficiency of nanoparticles (NPs) to tumors remains a challenge and hinders clinical translation. In this study, an artificial intelligence (AI)-assisted physiologically based pharmacokinetic (PBPK) model was developed to predict NPs' tumor delivery efficiency (DE) based on the physicochemical properties and experimental strategies. First, a generic PBPK model was applied to describe NPs’ tumor kinetics, and six different tumor-related parameters were determined. Second, machine learning (ML) and AI models were developed for predicting the tumor-related parameters. Incorporating the ML-predicted parameters into the PBPK model, an ML-assisted PBPK model was developed to predict the tumor kinetics of NPs. This generic PBPK model was applied to simulate the tumor kinetics, in which 114 out of 152 datasets (75%) achieved the determination coefficient (R 2 ) of ≥0.75, and the overall R 2 was 0.92. Distribution (PT) and permeability (PATC) coefficients at the tumor site were the most important parameters in predicting tumor DEs. The deep neural network (DNN) model was the best-performing model and selected for tumor-related parameter estimations. Targeting strategy and surface charge were determined as the important features for predicting various tumor-related PBPK parameters. External validation was conducted using an in vivo experiment, and half of the predicted concentrations were within the two-fold error of the observed data. This model can serve as a complementary tool for predicting tumor kinetics prior to animal experimentation, helping identify promising NP formulations and potentially improving the success rate of drug delivery.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence-Based Energy Optimization in 6G RANs Using Graph Deep Reinforcement Learning
items.abstract: This paper addresses AI-based cell sleep scheduling for dense 5G/6G radio access networks, where the central challenge is reducing energy consumption without degrading delay, blocking probability, or switching stability. The literature indicates growing interest in 3GPP and O-RAN energy-saving control, but many existing methods rely on local traffic thresholds or RL agents with weak spatial awareness. To address this gap, the paper proposes Graph-Aware Multi-Objective Sleep Scheduling (GMOSS), which combines graph neural encoding of inter-cell coupling with a dueling double DQN and a safety layer that filters overload-prone actions. Unlike generic GNN-RL controllers, GMOSS formulates cell sleep scheduling as a topology-aware constrained decision problem in which graph encoding, multi-objective value learning, and safety-constrained action projection are jointly used to prevent overload-prone sleep decisions before execution. A dense heterogeneous network with 19 cells is simulated under diurnal non-stationary traffic. Compared with Always-On, threshold control, independent DQN, and multi-agent DQN baselines, the proposed method achieves the best energy–QoS trade-off. Across 30 randomized seeds, GMOSS reduces average RAN power by 31.8% versus Always-On and 18.6% versus threshold control, improves energy efficiency to 1.058 Mbit/J, lowers blocking to 1.84%, and reduces switches per hour to 4.3. The gain in energy efficiency over independent DQN is 11.2% with a 95% confidence interval of [8.7%, 13.6%] and p < 0.001. The contribution of the paper lies in explicitly coupling spatial coordination, wake-up cost awareness, and practical safety constraints in a single AI controller that is well aligned with O-RAN style deployment.

items.title: Artificial intelligence-coupled paper-based detection of H2O2: an experiment customized from lab-on-paper sensing to image analysis to machine learning
items.abstract: Abstract Despite the vast growth of artificial intelligence (AI) in chemical research, educational programs have struggled to keep pace in familiarizing and preparing students for its implementation. In response to this gap, we have developed an interdisciplinary experiment for senior undergraduate and postgraduate students to discuss the implementations of AI in analytical chemistry with a focus on sensing. For this, an example paper-based fluorescent sensor was employed for the detection of H2O2 using image-based signal readout and machine learning-based concentration quantification. The Horseradish Peroxidase (HRP)-catalyzed yellow fluorescence emission resulting from the interaction of ortho-phenylenediamine (OPD) with H2O2 was recorded using smartphone cameras. Various features were extracted from the images and used to develop machine learning models for quantifying H2O2 concentration. Through this experiment, an introduction to sensing and paper-based sensor development, as well as the implementation of AI in sensor data analysis, was presented. During the lab experiment, students successfully developed Artificial Neural Network (ANN) models, validated them, and optimized them to improve performance. The feedback showed that students had become familiar with AI and machine learning and had increased interest in using AI in their future research.

items.title: Artificial intelligence-generated and algorithmically personalized music interventions and their effects on brain function, behavior, and health: a critical review
items.abstract: This critical review synthesizes empirical studies of algorithmically personalized and artificial-intelligence-generated music interventions reporting neurophysiological, neuroimaging, or objective behavioral outcomes. Literature was identified through structured searches of PubMed, Scopus, Google Scholar, IEEE Xplore, and the ACM Digital Library through 12 August 2026, with CNKI and Wanfang searched on 22 September 2026, supplemented by citation tracking. Twenty-one eligible studies (at least 1,005 participants) were identified. Five things the term artificial intelligence covers in this literature are separated: algorithmic selection from a corpus, rule-based sonification, parametric modulation of pre-existing material, machine-learning generative composition, and closed-loop delivery contingent on the listener’s own signal. Only three studies used a machine-learning generative model, so most of the evidence concerns algorithmic personalization of existing material. Studies of closed-loop neural systems reported the most consistent neurophysiological signal, and music-based alpha neurofeedback produced higher normalized alpha power than yoked random feedback. In an open-loop design, personalized EEG-derived music was reported to attenuate anxiety induction where self-selected preferred music and silence did not, with enhanced prefrontal theta oscillations as the associated correlate. Eight studies carried a comparator capable of isolating an algorithmic component from music exposure, and all eight favored the algorithmic condition. These eight address different causal questions, use different designs, and point to no single mechanism, so their results are best read as preliminary and hypothesis-generating. Evidence quality was very low throughout. The median reported sample size was 22, no study blinded participants or measured expectancy, and no specific finding has been independently replicated. GRADE certainty was very low for every outcome domain, covering EEG oscillatory power, sleep architecture, autonomic regulation, epileptiform activity, and cognitive, behavioral and affective outcomes. Neurophysiological change is reported more often than behavioral change, and behavioral change more often than clinical benefit. The evidence supports continued investigation and does not support clinical deployment. Eight reporting and design requirements for future trials are proposed.

items.title: Artificial intelligence–enabled Lean Six Sigma: a bibliometric and thematic review toward smart operational excellence
items.abstract: Purpose This study aims to examine the integration of artificial intelligence (AI) with Lean, Six Sigma and Lean Six Sigma (LSS) and develop a conceptual framework for AI-enabled operational excellence. Design/methodology/approach A combined bibliometric and thematic review was conducted using 52 Scopus-indexed journal articles. Publication trends, co-authorship, keyword co-occurrence, citation patterns and bibliographic coupling were integrated with qualitative thematic synthesis. Findings The field has progressed from Lean–Industry 4.0 alignment toward AI-enabled process improvement, LSS4.0, digitally enhanced define–measure–analyze–improve–control and decision intelligence. Five themes emerged: Lean digital transformation, AI-supported Six Sigma, LSS4.0 integration, AI-enabled decision intelligence and sustainability-oriented performance. Research limitations/implications The Scopus-only journal corpus may exclude relevant contributions. Future studies should empirically validate the framework and examine sector-specific applications and human–AI collaboration. Practical implications The framework guides organizations in aligning data infrastructure, AI capabilities, improvement routines, workforce competencies, leadership and governance when developing AI-enabled LSS systems. Social implications Responsible integration may support resource efficiency, sustainability, workforce development, transparency and accountability in AI-supported improvement decisions. Originality/value This study consolidates fragmented research into an evidence-informed framework connecting digital infrastructure, AI capability, process-improvement logic, organizational enablement and governance and value realization.

items.title: Artificial Obedience: How Large Language Models (LLMs) May Normalize Hierarchical Communication
items.abstract: This study introduces the concept of computer communication spillover: the transfer of interaction patterns from human–computer to human–human contexts via cue-triggered habit activation. The possibility of such transfer is supported by theories of power, habit formation, and social practice. Human interaction with large language models (LLMs) is here presented as a theoretical example, where the compliant nature of LLMs is central to the argument. We argue that by repeatedly occupying a superior, controlling position, LLM users may develop directive, instrumental, and control-oriented communication habits. Such habits might spill over to human-human communication contexts, where they could reduce politeness, tolerance for dissent, and openness to other people' perspectives. Because habits typically develop gradually, outside users’ awareness, spillover effects can raise ethical-legal questions about responsibility and human agency. Overall, we propose that computer communication spillover might be a broader societal risk of generative AI.

items.title: Assertion without a Speaker: Testimony, Tracking, and Large Language Models
items.abstract: Abstract Large language models produce assertion-shaped outputs that often bring their users to true belief. I argue for two conclusions of different strengths: that on the best current evidence, these systems do not transmit testimonial knowledge and that hearers are not now positioned to accord their outputs testimonial uptake, which does not wait on the first. From Burge, Williamson, Goldberg, Faulkner, and Lackey, I derive a Tracking Minimum: a source transmits testimonial knowledge that p only if the truth of p , or the evidential support for p , figures in the explanation of its producing that assertion, and does so in virtue of the source’s own production process rather than of a proxy on which that process depends. It is this endogeneity requirement, not any modal profile, that the five accounts share and current systems fail. The argument engages Burge’s extension of his framework to computational sources, the interpretability literature, and the published case for AI testimony, whose dispute with mine turns on an empirically decidable question, for which an experiment is specified. The positive proposal places LLM outputs within an extended epistemology of instruments, with a result that has gone unremarked: a working barometer satisfies the condition these systems fail.

items.title: Assistive and adaptive technologies for dyscalculia: a bibliometric review and narrative synthesis of AI-supported screening and learning support
items.abstract: PURPOSE: This study aimed to map the development of assistive and adaptive technology-supported approaches to dyscalculia between 2005 and 2025 and to clarify how artificial intelligence, adaptive learning, and assistive technologies are positioned within this research field. METHODS: A bibliometric review, complemented by a narrative synthesis, was conducted using 83 unique journal publications indexed in Web of Science and Scopus. The analysis included keyword frequency analysis, title-term distribution, keyword co-occurrence networks, thematic mapping, thematic evolution, and country-level collaboration analysis. RESULTS: The findings show that early research was largely grounded in neurocognitive explanations of dyscalculia, particularly numerical processing, working memory, and developmental learning difficulties. Recent publications indicate a broadening towards digital interventions, adaptive learning environments, serious games, augmented reality applications, and AI-supported assistive technologies. Studies using machine learning, deep learning, and probabilistic models suggest potential uses of AI for early screening, personalised feedback, individualised support, and cognitive support. However, AI remains an emerging rather than fully central organising theme. The review identified international collaboration patterns across Asia, the Middle East, Europe, and North America, alongside methodological and ethical issues, including limited longitudinal evidence, variability in intervention designs, biases in database and keyword selection, data privacy, and algorithmic transparency. CONCLUSIONS: Technology-assisted dyscalculia research has expanded from cognitive and developmental explanations towards more intervention-oriented, adaptive, and assistive technology-informed approaches. AI-supported assistive technologies appear promising for early identification, accessibility, individualised learning support, and participation in mathematics-related activities, but require stronger empirical validation, ethical implementation, user-centred evaluation, and integration into educational and rehabilitation-related support contexts.

items.title: Association of Musculoarticular Syndrome in Dental Assistants With Dental Chair Design: A Randomized Controlled Trial
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: Dental assistants are often susceptible to musculoskeletal disorders due to their professional duties; however, data on ergonomic risks for them are limited. AIM: To compare the severity of pain syndrome in dental assistants while working on chairs of different designs. METHODS: The study involved eight dental assistants who worked for two months on chairs of various designs and subjectively assessed pain severity using the visual analog scale (VAS). Before the start of each work shift, each assistant received one of two types of dental chair using a random number generator: a chair with armrests or a chair without armrests. Randomization was conducted independently for each shift and each participant. The resulting 221 observations were divided into two groups depending on the type of chair used during the shift: group 1 included 106 measurements obtained after a shift on a chair without armrests, and group 2 included 115 measurements obtained after a shift on a chair with armrests. Statistical analysis included assessment of normality of distribution (Shapiro–Wilk test), group comparisons (Student t-test, Mann–Whitney U test), and ROC analysis. Differences were considered statistically significant at p ≤ 0.05. RESULTS: Neck pain was the most common symptom in dental assistants (70%). Shoulder pain ranked second in frequency (52% of cases), and upper back pain ranked third (35%). When working on a chair with armrests, the median pain severity on the VAS was significantly lower in the neck (3.0 vs 5.0 points; p 0.001), right (3.0 vs 5.0 points; p 0.001) and left (2.5 vs 5.0 points; p 0.001) shoulders, as well as in the upper back on the right (4.0 vs 5.0 points; p = 0.030). For the upper back on the left, the differences did not reach statistical significance (p = 0.086). ROC analysis showed the best predictive ability of the model for the shoulders (AUC = 0.802 on the right; AUC = 0.804 on the left), moderate for the neck (AUC = 0.739–0.745) and the upper back on the right (AUC = 0.705). CONCLUSION: When comparing the groups, work on a chair with armrests was characterized by lower pain severity in the neck, shoulders, and upper back on the right than work on chairs of other designs.

items.title: Associations of hematological and biochemical parameters with radon exposure among male miners in China
items.abstract: Purpose Radon is a radioactive gas that produces a large amount of alpha particles during its decay process and a well-recognized health hazard, particularly an established risk factor for lung cancer in high-risk populations such as miners. Although hematological and biochemical parameters are useful indicators of human health status, the impact of radon exposure on these parameters among male miners remains unclear.Methods The participants of this study are 283 male miners in a tin mine in China. A targeted research design was adopted to conduct a questionnaire survey, physical examination, blood sample analysis coupled with radon concentration measurements, statistical analysis was performed to investigate the impact of varying levels of radon exposure on hematological and biochemical parameters among the participants.Results Mean platelet volume (MPV), plateletcrit (PCT), and platelet-large cell ratio (P-LCR) decreased significantly across the working-level month (WLM) groups (Bonferroni-corrected P < 0.003), as did albumin (ALB) and the albumin-to-globulin (A/G) ratio (Bonferroni-corrected P < 0.0045). In contrast, urea and aspartate aminotransferase (AST) increased significantly (Bonferroni-corrected P < 0.0045), whereas platelet count did not differ significantly among groups. Multiple linear regression confirmed WLM as an independent predictor for MPV (β= −0.282, P < 0.0001), PCT (β= −0.165, P = 0.010), P-LCR (β= −0.206, P = 0.002), urea (β = 0.178, P = 0.008), and platelet distribution width (β = 0.184, P = 0.006). All values remained within clinically normal reference ranges.Conclusion Cumulative occupational radon exposure was independently associated with decreased platelet volume indices and elevated urea levels in miners, suggesting subclinical hematological changes and altered renal-related parameters. MPV may serve as a candidate indicator requiring further validation of radiation-related hematopoietic alterations. These findings contribute to occupational health surveillance frameworks for populations chronically exposed to radon in mining environments.

items.title: Autonomous Agents Based on Large Language Models: Reasoning Strategies and Multi-Agent Interaction
items.abstract: Language-model agents acquire capability along two routes that published work almost always varies together, one enlarging the computation a single agent performs and the other enlarging the number of agents and the channels along which they pass partial results, which leaves the contribution of each route indistinguishable. This paper separates an agent system into a reasoning operator and an interaction topology, holding the number of agents fixed at three across all multi-agent topologies, together with the number of rounds, the message cap, the prompt skeleton, and the memory settings for all combinations, and evaluates a full factorial design of four reasoning levels and four topologies on three public test sets totalling 484 instances under five random seeds, giving 38,720 task executions. Comparisons are paired at the instance level, and effects are estimated from logistic mixed-effects models fitted to each test set separately. The reasoning factor spans 18.0 points on the static suite whereas the topology factor spans 7.8 points on the interactive one, a reversal indicating that the two mechanisms act on different failure modes. The topology span is taken across all four topology levels and therefore includes the step from one agent to three, against a structure-only span of 2.8 points among the multi-agent topologies. The two factors also depart from additivity in a localised manner. A mechanism-motivated single-degree-of-freedom contrast on the only cell in which both factors contribute a corrective pass is significant at p = 0.001 on the static suite, whereas the omnibus nine-degree-of-freedom interaction test is not (p = 0.094), and in that cell the observed 50.0 percent lies 5.8 points below the additive expectation. After tokens are counted, seven of the sixteen configurations remain undominated on the static suite and five on the operating-system suite, and returns saturate at 12,400 tokens per instance on the static suite under the present design.

items.title: Autonomous Forensic Systems Enabled by AI in Cybersecurity
items.abstract: The enormous amount of data that arrives daily from our personal gadgets, massive company networks, and cloud services has, in fact, caused a crisis for digital forensics. The conventional manual investigational methods, which were designed for a one-device-at-a-time world, cannot be used anymore. The “scaling problem” is not only about the number of cases but also about their complexity. In fact, investigators nowadays are having to face several terabytes of data; however, these are not only scattered across various cloud servers but are also encrypted and exist in a multitude of formats. The data is being produced and is changing at a very high speed, and at the same time, there is a strong and urgent demand to deliver the results quickly, which has, therefore, put forensic teams under enormous pressure and is, in fact, at the verge of a breaking point. The discipline is turning to automation, artificial intelligence (AI), and current computing frameworks in order to get out of this data blockade. The goal is to employ these technologies to perform those parts of the investigation that are extremely laborious, time-consuming, and tedious, such as data collection and filtering. Consequently, human analysts are freed from routine tasks and can therefore devote themselves to work with the most critical evidence. This transformation is facilitating the development of the new generation of forensic platforms, such as Autonomous Forensic Systems (AFS), which are designed for continuous monitoring and intelligent, adaptive decision-making. This paper discusses how the scaling problem has led digital forensics to change its way of working and how AI and cloud computing are increasingly becoming indispensable to the viability of investigations in our world, which is overloaded with data.

items.title: Behaviour analysis for large language model-driven agents
items.abstract: Understanding language-agent behaviour requires learning how actions are organised across a trajectory and how this organisation relates to context and outcomes. We propose a general framework that connects data-driven behavioural discovery with analysis and experimental investigation. Categories developed from recorded activity define what is measured. Analyses preserve the behaviours' positions in the process and express their relationships as interpretable hypotheses. Statistical assessment and tests in held-out contexts examine the strength and scope of the evidence. Experiments, including prompt steering, then test how behaviour and outcomes change under deliberately varied conditions. A study of iterative self-reflection illustrates how discovery, dependency learning and prompt comparisons can inform one another. We develop this approach for trajectories of varying length, event order and agent roles, and identify advances in coding, analysis and experimentation needed to support its wider use.

items.title: Beyond Correctness: How Novice Software Engineering Students Exercise Oversight of Generative AI
items.abstract: Generative AI (GenAI) is shifting software engineering students' work from producing artefacts towards evaluating and supervising AI-generated outputs. However, little is known about what characteristics students identify in outputs when reporting interventions, or how they exercise oversight during authentic software engineering work. We analysed 962 student-AI interaction turns documented by 145 first-year software engineering students through structured AI Journals, including 172 student-declared interventions. Using a multi-dimensional coding framework, we characterised the output characteristics identified in these reported interventions, students' reasons for intervening, the actions they took, and how those actions were enacted. Fitness problems were identified in 74.4% of interventions, compared with 16.9% involving correctness problems, indicating that oversight more often concerned whether plausible AI outputs were suitable for the engineering task than whether they contained explicit errors. Among classifiable interventions, students most frequently modified generated outputs (51.0%) or refined their prompts (28.2%), with both response types commonly associated with engineering fit. Within-student analysis further showed that outputs perceived as containing minor flaws were associated with lower evaluation confidence than outputs perceived as perfect. Taken together, these findings characterise novice AI oversight as a process that extends beyond error detection to encompass both judgement of fitness for purpose and active intervention in AI-assisted engineering work.

items.title: Beyond Coverage and Mutation: A Blind-Spot Analysis of LLM-Generated Unit Tests
items.abstract: Existing evaluation protocols for unit tests rely on aggregate metrics such as branch coverage and mutation score. These metrics quantify the extent to which a test suite exercises program behavior, but do not identify the behavioral obligations it systematically leaves unchecked. We propose BlindSpotEval, an obligation-based evaluation framework aligned with the Arrange-Act-Assert pattern. The framework comprises three metrics, Boundary-Value Adequacy, Control-Flow Adequacy, and Oracle Strength, complemented by an assessment of execution reliability. We also introduce ObligBench, a complexity-stratified Java benchmark comprising 895 complex and 700 low-complexity functions with source-side obligation annotations. Evaluating 14,320 tests from four LLMs under four prompting strategies reveals systematic blind spots. Incorrect assertions account for 15.6% of test failures, illustrating that coverage alone does not establish oracle correctness. Among executable tests, coverage of null, negative, and empty arguments reaches only 34.8%, 23.8%, and 38.8%, compared with average coverage above 93% for booleans. Catch blocks and default groups have Control-Flow Adequacy scores of only 0.100 and 0.312. Across both dimensions, LLM-generated tests exhibit the happy-path bias observed in human-written tests, concentrating on normal inputs and expected flows while leaving unusual values and exceptional paths unchecked. Oracle strength is high on average but uneven, with weaker assertions for object return property values and exceptions. These blind spots also occur in low-complexity functions, suggesting that code complexity alone does not explain them. BlindSpotEval provides construct-level adequacy profiles that identify under-tested obligation types and can guide targeted improvements beyond those supported by aggregate scores alone.

items.title: Beyond Data Schedule: Fast LLM Pretraining on Data Mixtures by Loss-Reweighting
items.abstract: Large language models often acquire specialized capabilities through successive pretraining stages, but these gains can come at the cost of forgetting earlier knowledge. In this work, we investigate whether such trade-offs can be improved by changing how strongly each domain contributes to learning while keeping its data exposure fixed. We find that, in controlled knowledge--mathematics experiments, loss reweighting produces a single checkpoint that surpasses the best knowledge and reasoning scores attained along either stage trajectory. This reveals an independent control that data-mixture ratios alone do not capture. Building on this finding, we propose LARE (Loss-Adaptive Reweighting under fixed Exposure), which automatically adjusts domain weights from running loss statistics. Motivated by a theoretical analysis of gradient noise, its normalized inverse-square-root rule balances relative loss scales without changing the sampled mixture or requiring additional runs to search for weights. Across knowledge, mathematics, and code, \Method{} improves all five evaluated benchmarks for a 1.5B model trained on 240B tokens, averaging +7.84 pp over a matched direct mixture, including gains of +17.06 pp on GSM8K and +9.00 pp on MATH. These findings demonstrate that adjusting domain loss scales can improve joint capabilities without additional domain exposure.

items.title: Beyond Gain: Measuring Skill Internalization for Agent Skill Retirement
items.abstract: LLM agents retrieve skills from public hubs that hold up to about 100,000 entries and serve many models. As models improve, a hub must find the skills a given model has internalized, meaning it can do without them, and retire them for that model, yet internalization has not been measured with known reliability. Published rules that compare runs with and without a skill retire on the gain alone. The gain is near zero both for an internalized skill and when neither the model nor the skill delivers the capability, a state we call uncovered. We instead withhold the skill, score the model on a task synthesized from it, and trust a high unaided score only when another model gains from the skill, since nearly half of high scores come from tasks no model benefits from. Under four models, a published gain rule applied with one task per skill removes over half of the uncovered skills. On SkillsBench, 28 of its 31 retirements rest on probes no run passed in full, while retiring on the unaided score costs no detectable reward. Unaided verdicts reproduce across tasks more often than the gain rule's (Cohen's kappa 0.42 against 0.23) but differ across models, so a hub must read them per model. We release 1,251 skills with tasks and item scores under four models.

items.title: Beyond Human–AI interaction: exploring the influence of AI anthropomorphism on work engagement
items.abstract: Purpose This study examines how anthropomorphic cues that make AI agency socially salient influence employee work engagement in mandatory, performance-oriented human–AI collaboration. It distinguishes AI agency from AI anthropomorphism, tests affective and evaluative motivational mechanisms and identifies perceived AI threat as a boundary condition grounded in the Job Demands-Resources (JD-R) model. Design/methodology/approach Across two pilot studies and two main experiments (total N = 501), we used immersive workplace role-playing scenarios to test a dual-pathway model. Integrating social response theory with the JD-R model, this research tests a dual-pathway model in which anthropomorphic design influences work engagement through emotional bonding and acquisitive impression management motive (IMM), whereas perceived artificial intelligence threat operates as a hindrance demand that weakens these resource pathways. Findings Anthropomorphic AI enhanced work engagement through two motivational routes: an affective route via emotional bonding and an evaluative route via IMM. However, perceived AI threat significantly attenuated these benefits. When threat was high, the positive effects of anthropomorphism on emotional bonding, IMM and work engagement became non-significant, suggesting that replacement-related threat drains the psychological capacity needed for anthropomorphic cues to function as job resources. Originality/value This research contributes to workplace AI and information systems (IS) scholarship by clarifying how anthropomorphic cues make AI agency socially salient without equating anthropomorphism with agency. It extends prior work on anthropomorphic AI and engagement by identifying an evaluative pathway – performing for AI – alongside the affective pathway of bonding with AI. It also offers a contingency-based explanation for the anthropomorphism paradox by showing that the benefits of humanlike design depend on the surrounding AI-threat climate.

items.title: Beyond moonlighting: side-gigs and employee performance
items.abstract: Purpose We examine how types of secondary activities relate to primary job performance under bounded rationality and when managers should permit, encourage, or restrict them. Design/methodology/approach Using an archival dataset from professional baseball (1945–2018), we classify secondary activities as unrelated, teaching-related, or learning-related. We estimate Ordinary Least Squares and difference-in-differences models around the 1965 Major League Baseball (MLB) draft and measure performance with Wins Above Replacement Findings Unrelated and teaching-related secondary activities are associated with lower performance, whereas learning-related secondary activities are associated with higher performance than teaching-related secondary activities. When the job becomes more salient, these negative associations intensify, while the performance advantage of learning-related secondary activities widens. Research limitations/implications Evidence derives from a single industry and an observational setting. The cognitively aligned typology and boundary-condition logic refine Behavioral Theory of the Firm accounts of attention allocation and offer testable extensions. Practical implications Rather than adopting blanket rules, managers should evaluate secondary activities according to their cognitive demands, intensity, alignment with the focal role, and demonstrated performance consequences, and revisit these evaluations as the stakes of the primary role rise. Social implications Differentiated policies, coupled with equitable skill-building alternatives, can enhance worker wellbeing while protecting core performance. Originality/value We move beyond the “secondary activity versus no secondary activity” view by testing a cognitively aligned typology and its moderators, translating Behavioral Theory of the Firm into actionable policy guidance.

items.title: Beyond question and answer: Practical applications of multimodal and multifunctional large language models in ophthalmology with a scoping review and future directions
items.abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) connect language understanding with image-based reasoning and are increasingly explored as artificial intelligence systems for ophthalmic image analysis, workflow support, research prototyping, and education. This scoping review synthesizes 21 peer-reviewed studies that moved beyond text-only question answering to evaluate visual question answering (VQA), domain-adapted or fine-tuned ophthalmic models, retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), and low- or no-code tools for analytics and prototype development. Across studies, the evidence suggests early feasibility for image-conditioned explanations, triage support, documentation assistance, structured data extraction, and rapid tool creation. However, the evidence base remains heterogeneous and preliminary, with mixed diagnostic performance, variable prompts and model versions, limited external validation, and persistent risks including reasoning errors, hallucinations, session variability, privacy concerns, and security threats. To illustrate potential workflows not yet fully covered by the literature, we also provide clearly labeled author-built demonstrations, which are non-evidentiary, for fundus and optical coherence tomography (OCT)-based VQA, optical character recognition (OCR) tabulation, code-free analytics, automated software programming, and web-based risk calculators. Future priorities include extending image-conditioned reasoning to additional ophthalmic modalities, strengthening RAG with curated corpora and provenance, evaluating few-shot and in-context learning for rare conditions, and using controlled generative imaging for education and data augmentation. Overall, MLLMs may support supervised ophthalmic artificial intelligence applications in selected clinical, research, and educational workflows. Clinical deployment will require external validation, prospective human-in-the-loop evaluation, standards-based workflow integration, privacy-preserving infrastructure, audit logging, cybersecurity, and post-deployment monitoring.

items.title: Beyond smart cities: rethinking urban AI for inclusive development in the Global South
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly shaping urban development across the Global South, offering opportunities to improve planning, public services, and resource management. However, AI-enabled systems operate within existing inequalities in infrastructure, representation, institutional capacity, and digital participation. This article argues that digital access alone is insufficient for inclusive urban AI. Drawing on data-justice scholarship and illustrative cases, it examines how AI can create uneven opportunities and risks for vulnerable populations. It calls for a context-sensitive approach that prioritises representative data, meaningful participation, accountability, human oversight, and safeguarding, ensuring that technological innovation contributes to more inclusive and equitable urban development outcomes.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

items.title: BEYOND TECHNOSTRESS AI Fatigue as a Cumulative Adaptation Burden in Education and Work
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence has become a persistent layer of work and learning rather than an occasional tool. Users must repeatedly decide when to delegate, how to prompt, whether to trust, how to verify, and how responsibility should be distributed. This integrative review defines AI fatigue as a cumulative reduction in the cognitive, affective, or motivational capacity for adaptive AI engagement when interaction, evaluation, correction, learning, and role-adjustment demands accumulate faster than recovery and support. The review connects technostress, automation vigilance, cognitive load and offloading, trust calibration, digital fatigue, and the Job Demands–Resources perspective. It introduces an Exposure–Adaptation–Depletion–Response framework, a five-domain taxonomy, and an AI Fatigue Load model that separates use volume from uncertainty, task stakes, correction burden, interruption, role disruption, and imposed adoption velocity. The analysis is updated to incorporate a 2026 validated 15-item AI Fatigue Scale; the proposed load model complements that psychophysiological outcome measure by specifying socio-technical antecedents and exposure conditions. Educational and organizational applications show why AI may simultaneously improve output and worsen human sustainability. The article identifies recurring inferential errors, presents a measurement and longitudinal research agenda, and proposes an intervention hierarchy spanning interface design, workflow, curriculum, organizational policy, and governance. AI fatigue is positioned neither as generic screen tiredness nor as a synonym for burnout, but as an adaptation problem located in the coupled human–AI–institution system.

items.title: BEYOND THE CLASSROOM: ANALYZING THE FACTORS AFFECTING GRADE 12 LEARNERS’ COLLEGE COURSE PREFERENCES
items.abstract: This study utilized a quantitative descriptive-survey and correlational-predictive research design to systematically examine the variables dictating the college preferences of graduating senior high school learners. Conducted at Mindanao State University - Lanao National College of Arts and Trades (MSU-LNCAT) during the School Year 2025–2026, the investigation relied on a total seventy-three Grade 12 learner-respondents comprising of forty-three Humanities and Social Sciences Learner-respondents (58.90%) and thirty TVL track learner-respondents (41.10%), with a demographic concentration of fifty-six females (76.71%) and seventeen males (23.29%). Data was gathered via face-to-face classroom administration using a structured 5-point Likert scale questionnaire evaluating three predictive dimensions: Intrinsic Motivation, Familial Influence, and Peer Dynamics and Social Media Influence. Descriptive and inferential statistical treatments was used including frequency, percentage, weighted mean, standard deviation, item ranking, and the Pearson (r) Correlation Coefficient. Intrinsic Motivation emerged as the primary driver, yielding a high composite mean of 3.92 (High Influence) and a Significant Strong Positive Relationship, with course preferences, successfully rejecting the null hypothesis. Conversely, external factors had minimal impact; Familial Influence acted strictly as a secondary, consultative reference point with a neutral composite mean of 3.39 (Moderate Influence) and a weak, variable correlation, while Peer Dynamics and Social Media Influence exerted the weakest pressure, finishing with a low composite mean of 2.68 (Low Influence) and No Significant Relationship. Ultimately, these findings demonstrate that modern Grade 12 learner-respondents at MSU-LNCAT exercise high psychological autonomy, systematically prioritizing internal passion and specialized tracking competencies over parental expectations, peer circles, or digital trends.

items.title: Beyond What to Say: Proactive Utterance Timing with Inner Thoughts for Werewolf Agents
items.abstract: Participating in a conversation involves not only deciding what to say but also whether to speak at all. This judgment carries even greater significance in environments like the Werewolf game, where participants' interests conflict, because both utterances and silence are subject to interpretation and assessment by others. Therefore, determining when to speak, as well as what to say, is crucial for an LLM agent playing the Werewolf game. In this study, we introduce a Werewolf AI agent developed for the Anytime Utterance Track of the AIWolfDial shared task. Our system builds on the existing Inner Thoughts framework, which determines utterance timing during conversations by generating internal thoughts and evaluating the value of each thought for expression at that moment. Since existing methods were designed for general dialogue, we have redesigned the system specifically for the competitive environment and incomplete information setting of Werewolf games. We call our adapted method Adversarial Inner Thoughts. Through experiments involving analysis of self-play logs and human evaluations, we analyze and discuss the effectiveness of our approach.

items.title: Big data and artificial intelligence in digital marketing
items.abstract: Big Data and artificial intelligence are changing digital marketing through consumer behavior analysis, personalized communication, and automation. This paper examines their role in marketing processes, performance measurement, and the conditions for application in Serbia. A narrative review of selected literature is combined with a descriptive analysis of published statistics on ICT use, e-commerce, and enterprise AI adoption. The analysis identifies widespread consumer participation in digital channels alongside more limited enterprise adoption of AI. Serbia remains below the EU average in enterprise AI use, although above some member states. The paper’s contribution lies in linking data resources, analytical capabilities, and managerial competencies to explain why technology adoption alone is insufficient for effective digital marketing. Practical implications emphasize employee development, responsible data management, and the evaluation of marketing outcomes. The findings should be interpreted within the limits of aggregate indicators, which do not directly measure marketing-specific AI use or its effectiveness. Future research should examine these applications and their outcomes at the enterprise level.

items.title: Bounded Delegation: How Student Design Teams Keep Strategic Control over Generative AI
items.abstract: Generative AI is increasingly embedded in team-based design, yet little is known about how teams negotiate its role over extended projects. We conducted a four-week situated study with nine graduate design teams (54 students) developing complete murder mystery Live Action Role-Playing games. Using domestication theory as a sensitizing framework, we analyzed 104 human-AI collaboration events, project outputs, and 27 semi-structured interviews. We identified three collaboration modes: Task-Based Empowered Creation, AI-Augmented Creative Co-creation, and Progressive Trust-Informed Collaboration. A fourth mode, Ceding Executive Trust Collaboration, was theoretically possible but did not occur. Across teams, AI was delegated tactical tasks such as content and asset generation, while humans retained control over narrative direction, quality standards, and core mechanics. We conceptualize this pattern as bounded delegation within a strategic-tactical hierarchy, offering an alternative to linear autonomy-progression models and informing AI tools that support rather than supplant human strategic control.

items.title: Bounding Queue Waits for Fair Scheduling of Bursty HPC Workloads via Hierarchical Algorithms
items.abstract: HPC clusters are shared among many projects, each holding an allocation of node-hours, and ensuring fairness is becoming harder. Foundation models workflows and automated pipelines have made job submissions bursty and concentrated among a few heavy users, so occasional users absorb queueing delays created by frequent ones, with no indication of how long their jobs will wait. Existing schedulers either forget past usage, protect only the job at the head of the queue, or assume that running jobs can be preempted. We propose HyDRA, a Hybrid Deadline and Ranking-Aware scheduler that enforces fairness among users while bounding the queue wait of every job. HyDRA assigns each job a deadline on arrival based on its size, the priorities of its project and user, the current backlog, and how far its project and user are from their entitled share. It ranks waiting jobs by a priority score that grows with waiting time, serves jobs close to their deadlines first, and backfills a job only when no deadline, or fairness limit is violated. We evaluate HyDRA on workloads derived from a year of ALCF Polaris job traces, against conventional schedulers and variants inspired by PCS, Themis, and the PBS job-sort formula used at ALCF. HyDRA achieves $2\times$ the project-level Jain's fairness of the best baseline, starts 47\% of jobs by their deadlines compared with at most 36\% for the baselines even for largest workloads, and lowers the 95th-\%ile bounded slowdown by 4.2$\times$ relative to the next best baseline, at a moderate cost in utilization.

items.title: Building Permit Automatability: A Multi-Level Analysis of Thuringia
items.abstract: The automation of administrative decision-making is increasingly important in digital building permitting. Yet research mainly addresses technically formalisable requirements and rarely examines automation potential across administrative workflows and legal decision situations. This study analyses the Thuringian building permitting process in Germany through a multi-level, process-oriented framework covering planning law, building regulations, procedural rules, and administrative procedure law. The workflow was decomposed into seven modules and 163 decision sub-steps, classified as deterministic algorithm-based, LLM-supported, or non-automatable. Results show marked differences across procedural stages and regulatory layers. items.title: Campaigns That Click: Unleashing the Power of Push Notifications on Mobile Apps
items.abstract: As mobile apps increasingly mediate digital engagement, push notifications have emerged as a key tool for directing user attention, yet systematic evidence on their behavioral and ecosystem-level effects remains limited. Using data from over 200 push campaigns and 60 million user-campaign observations on a leading U.S. mobile-offer marketplace, we combine large-scale observational analyses with controlled experiments to study how push notifications shape user engagement. We find that push notifications significantly increase same-day click-throughs to advertised merchants, with substantial heterogeneity across merchant characteristics, user characteristics, message design, and delivery timing. Beyond focal-merchant responses, notifications are associated with increased engagement with non-advertised merchants both within and across categories, suggesting that push notifications reshape attention across the marketplace ecosystem. Both the large-scale empirical analysis and controlled experiments yield evidence consistent with two complementary mechanisms—content-driven processing of notification information and reminder-based attention activation. The results also identify attentional saturation as a key boundary condition—repeated exposure produces diminishing responsiveness and may even reduce engagement at high notification frequencies. These findings position push notifications as a mobile-native attention-allocation lever that platforms can strategically deploy, while underscoring the need to balance engagement gains against user fatigue and attention costs.

items.title: Can AI Agents Help Robotic Engineers? Lessons from Two Focus Days in Industry
items.abstract: Software developers increasingly use AI agents that execute multi-step programming tasks on their own. However, it is unclear if and how this transfers to robotic engineering, where engineers program industrial robots in niche, vendor-specific languages and rely on visual feedback from simulation tools. Within this paper, we report a case study on the use of AI agents by an SME that programs industrial robots. Our results show that the agent did not make the engineers more productive, with the exception of a task that required the generation of highly repetitive code. However, the results with the agent improved over time, as the engineers learned how to use it and the agent was adapted to the domain. Moreover, the experience with AI mattered more for the success with the agent than the experience with robotic engineering. This shows that AI agents are not a plug-and-play solution. Instead, companies must train their engineers on the usage of agents, plan time for a learning curve, and ensure that agent configurations match the domain and developer requirements. The strong learning curve we observed further implies that studies on productivity gains with AI should be longitudinal, as they otherwise miss how engineers adopt agents in practice.

items.title: Can education set the agenda for AI? Simulated innovation and pedagogical direction-setting in teacher education
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) creates a critical inflection point in the relationship between educational innovation and technological development. For decades, educational systems have often been positioned reactively: technologies emerge, institutions search for their possible pedagogical uses, and teacher education programmes adapt belatedly to tools designed elsewhere. This article argues that GenAI makes this sequence increasingly insufficient. Because GenAI can produce texts, explanations, feedback, learning resources, and assessment artefacts that resemble evidence of educational performance, it compels education to define more clearly what should count as learning, authorship, judgement, and valid evidence. The article develops the concept of simulated innovation to describe technology-led change that signals modernisation without transforming pedagogical purposes, assessment logics, teacher judgement, student agency, or learning relationships. It then argues that GenAI opens the possibility of pedagogical direction-setting: beginning from educational, ethical, epistemic, and democratic aims, and requiring technology to respond to those aims. Teacher education is positioned as a strategic site for this shift, not because teachers alone can govern AI-mediated education, but because professional formation can prepare educators to translate pedagogical purposes into criteria for design, assessment, ethical judgement, and technology governance.

items.title: Can LLM Annotators Match Human Consistency? Benchmarking Human Agreement and Optimizing Multi-Agent with Contrastive Knowledge
items.abstract: LLM-based annotation has advanced rapidly, yet existing benchmarks remain misaligned with real-world practice. Actual annotation often involves lengthy, task-specific guidelines, and different annotators may produce divergent but reasonable judgments, especially on boundary cases, where single-labeled dataset fail to reflect this disagreement. This gap also limits existing single-agent and workflow-based annotation systems, which often lack adaptability to complex, evolving guidelines. To bridge this gap, we introduce ANT-A Benchmark, a real-world multi-annotator benchmark spanning 7 datasets across domains and modalities, with task-specific guidelines and 5 independent human labels per instance. ANT-A enables a distribution-aware evaluation, using Fleiss kappa to assess how closely model annotations align with human labeling distributions. We further propose ANT-OR, a multi-agent annotation framework that refines prompts by distilling contrastive decision rules from positive and negative feedback. Experiments show that ANT-OR improves agreement@>=2 accuracy by 4.5 points over the strongest baseline and achieves the highest alignment with human annotator distributions as measured by Fleiss kappa within 2 points. Code and benchmark are available at https://github.com/Krueske/ANT-OR.

items.title: Case Studies of Major Cyberterrorism Incidents
items.abstract: The exponential growth of artificial intelligence is changing digital forensics and cybersecurity at a much faster rate than traditional tools and methodologies can be updated. AI is now at the center of both defense and attack strategies; thus, investigators and security professionals have to reconsider every stage of evidence handling, threat detection, and incident response. This chapter reviews how AI-driven models are changing the forensic department by accomplishing the tasks of data acquisition, log correlation, malware analysis, behavioral profiling, and attribution with the help of automation, accuracy, and scalability that were unheard of before. Also, it accepts the uncomfortable truth that AI is a factor that escalates the complexity level of cyber threats. Opponents are equipping generative models, reinforcement learning, and automated vulnerability discovery to develop attacks that are adaptive, evasive, and quicker than humans, in the loop systems can respond to. The chapter goes on to explain how the dual-use character of AI is one of the main reasons behind the operational benefits, as well as the new kinds of risks that are highlighted. It signals a time when digital forensics will have to evolve to be able to analyses synthetic media, autonomous malware, large-scale IoT environments, and complex data streams in which they will not be able to use the traditional forensic frameworks that have never been designed for these kinds of tasks. Moreover, this chapter provides solutions to legal, ethical, and policy issues faced by AI-generated evidence, algorithmic bias, explainability gaps, and accountability problems arising during forensic investigations. The chapter acts as a futuristic lens to the changing face of the investigative strategies, cyber defense architectures, and the worldwide threat landscape due to AI over the next ten years. Consequently, this chapter serves as a practical guide for scientists, professionals, and decision-makers who have to change their ways swiftly or be at a disadvantage.

items.title: CASE: Confusion-Aware Skill Evolution for Frozen Multimodal Emotion Models
items.abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have substantially advanced Multimodal Emotion Recognition (MER) by enabling fine-grained emotion understanding through reasoning over multimodal evidence. However, they still exhibit systematic confusion between semantically adjacent emotions with highly overlapping multimodal cues. Existing approaches typically address these errors through global parameter adaptation, making confusion correction costly and inflexible. We instead observe that emotion confusion is highly localized and therefore better addressed through reusable pair-specific expertise. Building on this insight, we propose Confusion-Aware Skill Evolution (CASE), the first agent-skill framework for MER. CASE maintains a sparse, self-evolving library of pair-specific EmotionSkills that externalize affective expertise from model parameters, enabling the learned expertise to be continuously refined and readily transferred across diverse frozen MLLM backbones. During inference, CASE dynamically retrieves the appropriate EmotionSkill to reinforce boundary-aware reasoning while keeping the MLLM backbone frozen. Extensive experiments on CA-MER, DFEW, and EMER demonstrate the effectiveness and transferability of CASE across both general-purpose and emotion-specialized MLLMs. Notably, CASE improves the average accuracy of Qwen3-VL-8B on the CA-MER benchmark from 46.80% to 59.13%, while achieving consistent gains across MLLMs.

items.title: CauProphet: Teaching Agents to Develop Causal Cognition like Humans
items.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents increasingly support long-horizon tasks by leveraging external memory and past experience. However, existing agents mainly retrieve records or summaries, lacking the ability to form and refine causal understanding of the world. Inspired by human causal cognition, we introduce CauProphet, an agent that develops and updates causal knowledge within its Causal Cognition. For each task, CauProphet combines relevant knowledge in Causal Cognition with current evidence to construct a Causal Belief, a structured belief capturing causal factors and the effects of possible actions. It uses this belief for decision-making and continuously updates both the belief and Causal Cognition as new observations emerge, enabling causal knowledge that persists beyond individual experiences. Evaluations demonstrate that CauProphet progressively acquires causal knowledge and transfers it to future decision-making. In financial research, CauProphet leverages prior discoveries to improve downstream analyses and outperforms all baselines in mean rank correlation with next-day returns, achieving a 25.4% improvement over a baseline agent. It also improves prediction accuracy from 21.3% to 28.6% in dynamic real-world settings. Further experiments validate its ability to perform reliable causal analysis and action selection across scientific and everyday tasks, demonstrating the potential of causal experience learning for next-generation LLM agents.

items.title: CEMIR vs. FISER: a comparative study of reasoning-based and enrichment-based approaches to pragmatic intent recognition
items.abstract: Intent recognition in human-robot interaction requires agents to resolve ambiguous natural language instructions by inferring the speaker's underlying goals. Research has increasingly focused on two notable paradigms for addressing this task: structured symbolic reasoning and multimodal input enrichment. However, it remains unclear whether enrichment-based methods provide benefit in settings where the ambiguity concerns unstated human intent rather than missing observable scene information. In this paper, we present a comparative and diagnostic study benchmarking FISER - a framework utilizing structured social and embodied reasoning - against CEMIR (Context-Enriched Multimodal Intent Recognition), a method that performs multimodal enrichment by synthesizing narratives and photorealistic images from textual prompts. By evaluating both approaches across four Large Language Models (LLMs), ranging from Qwen2.5-Omni-3B to GPT-5, on the HandMeThat v2 benchmark, we analyze their capability to resolve pragmatic ambiguities. Our statistical analysis, employing multiple-comparison correction, reveals no statistically significant difference in performance between FISER and CEMIR across any model or difficulty level. This pattern holds across all sixteen model-by-difficulty comparisons, as well as in a targeted ablation isolating CEMIR's narrative and visual components. Instead, performance is primarily associated with backbone capability and the inherent difficulty of the ambiguity. These findings suggest a boundary condition for text-derived multimodal enrichment: when the relevant task constraints are already available in the textual instruction, synthetic multimodal augmentation may not provide measurable benefit over structured reasoning on the same text.

items.title: Challenges and opportunities in using digital health technologies for decision-making in prehospital non-emergency situations in Norway: a qualitative study
items.abstract: Abstract Background Norway has a well-established emergency care system and prehospital infrastructure. However, an ageing population and the increasing prevalence of chronic diseases create a growing need to explore how digital health technologies may support decision-making in prehospital non-emergency situations. While technologies such as telehealth, remote monitoring, wearables, portable medical devices, communication platforms, and Artificial Intelligence-based decision-support systems have shown promise for supporting prehospital decision-making, their implementation in Norway remains limited. This study explored Norwegian paramedics’ perceptions of the challenges and opportunities of using digital health technologies to support decision-making in prehospital non-emergency situations. Methods An exploratory qualitative interview study was conducted to investigate paramedics’ experiences and perceptions of digital health technology use in decision-making during prehospital non-emergency situations in Norway. Data were collected through 12 semi-structured interviews with paramedics involved in Norwegian ambulance care. Participants were recruited using purposive and snowball sampling. Interviews were audio-recorded, transcribed verbatim, and analysed using reflexive thematic analysis following Braun and Clarke’s six-phase framework. NVivo 15 and Microsoft Excel were used to support data organization and analysis. Results Four themes captured challenges and opportunities of digital health technologies in prehospital non-emergency situations: digital support for call assessment and ambulance resource allocation; digital patient information for shared situational awareness; digital communication for interprofessional consultation and care coordination; and digital diagnostics for conveyance and non-conveyance decisions. Participants reported fragmented information systems, restricted access to patient records, limitations in communication technologies, and insufficient diagnostic support. They identified opportunities involving video-supported assessment, interoperable patient information, real-time clinical data sharing, multiparty consultation, and point-of-care diagnostics. However, the perceived value of these technologies depended on their reliability, usability, and integration with professional roles and healthcare services. Conclusions Digital health technologies were perceived as having the potential to support decision-making in prehospital non-emergency situations by reducing uncertainty and supporting appropriate care pathways. Their perceived value depended on reliable information, interoperability, usable communication, diagnostic support, and clear cross-service responsibilities. Digital transformation should therefore prioritise integrated, context-sensitive systems that augment paramedics’ professional judgement and may enable timely, coordinated, and patient-centred care while remaining responsive to evolving clinical needs and care environments.

The chapter emphasizes that protecting client agency, engagement, and self-efficacy requires careful consideration of when and how AI is incorporated into therapeutic contexts.

items.title: Changes in the acceptance of artificial intelligence in medicine among physicians and the general public in Japan: A repeated cross-sectional comparison of 2018 and 2025
items.abstract: Medical artificial intelligence (AI) has advanced rapidly, yet whether growing societal familiarity with AI is accompanied by greater willingness to receive relatively autonomous AI-led care remains unclear. We conducted repeated cross-sectional online surveys in Japan in 2018 and 2025 using the same questionnaire and compared self-identified physicians and members of the general public (2018: 399 physicians and 600 members of the public; 2025: 300 physicians and 300 members of the public). Mean responses to the item assessing intention to use medical AI did not differ significantly between survey years in either group, despite consistently favorable evaluations of its usefulness and future necessity. Among physicians, the unadjusted mean response regarding the potential of medical AI to improve clinical efficiency was higher in 2025, but this difference was not significant after adjustment for age and sex. Among members of the public, self-rated knowledge of medical AI was higher in 2025, while expectations that medical AI would increase healthcare costs were also greater. These findings suggest that increased self-rated knowledge may not necessarily be accompanied by greater intention to use relatively autonomous medical AI. Implementation strategies should therefore address concerns regarding responsibility, safety, data protection, and healthcare costs alongside efforts to improve public understanding.

items.title: ChatGPT-assisted mathematics learning in the era of generative AI: A bibliometric analysis of research trends, collaboration networks, and emerging pedagogical themes
items.abstract: Purpose – This study aims to map the development of research on ChatGPT-assisted mathematics learning during the 2023–2025 period. Methodology – This study uses bibliometric analysis to examine the intellectual, social, and conceptual structures of research on ChatGPT-assisted mathematics learning. Data were obtained from the Scopus database and analyzed using Bibliometrix Biblioshiny. Document selection followed the PRISMA 2020 reporting guidelines as a checklist for the identification, screening, eligibility, and inclusion stages. Of the 1,227 documents identified, 143 met the inclusion criteria and were analyzed further. Findings – The number of publications increased from 12 in 2023 to 36 in 2024 and 95 in 2025, indicating an annual growth rate of 181.37% and an average of 18.63 citations per document. International co-authorship accounted for only 16.78% of these documents, indicating limited cross-national collaboration. ChatGPT, mathematics education, and artificial intelligence were the most dominant keywords, while geometry, prospective mathematics teachers, and personalized learning were relatively underrepresented. Novelty – Unlike previous studies that generally treat ChatGPT as part of generative artificial intelligence, this research analytically positions ChatGPT-assisted mathematics learning as a separate bibliometric unit and proposes AI-mediated mathematics learning as a conceptual proposition that emphasizes critical validation of AI-generated results. Significance – These findings provide an evidence-based research agenda to strengthen international collaboration and develop mathematics instruction that emphasizes reasoning, justification, and critical evaluation of AI-generated solutions, while identifying priorities for future empirical research.

items.title: Climate Change and Workers’ Health and Safety: An Umbrella Review
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: This umbrella review synthesizes current evidence on the health and safety impacts of climate change among workers. In particular, it aims to identify the main workers' categories at the highest risk, the main health and safety outcomes, methodological limitations, and future directions reported in the literature, as well as preventive strategies described in recent reviews. METHODS: A comprehensive search was conducted in PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science. Systematic and scoping reviews addressing climate-related occupational health and safety outcomes were included. Study selection and data extraction were performed independently by two reviewers. Methodological quality was assessed using the ROBIS tool, and findings were synthesized in accordance with PRISMA and PRIOR guidelines. RESULTS: Most of the available evidence concerns outdoor occupations, particularly agriculture and construction, where exposure to high temperatures is associated with increased risks of injuries and heat strain. Emerging data also highlight links with mental health, renal disease, and chronic conditions. However, the literature remains fragmented, with few meta-analyses and substantial heterogeneity. Preventive strategies have been proposed, but their implementation remains inconsistent. CONCLUSIONS: Evidence confirms that climate change has become a determinant of occupational health and safety. Future research should strengthen methodological coherence, adopt longitudinal approaches, and address vulnerable populations.
topics: Occupational Health and Safety in Workplaces

items.title: Clinical integration of artificial intelligence for diagnosis, risk prediction and management of rare cardiovascular diseases
items.abstract: Abstract Introduction RCDs comprise a diverse group of inherited and acquired disorders characterized by low prevalence, substantial genetic and phenotypic heterogeneity, delayed diagnosis, and limited evidence-based therapeutic options. These challenges contribute to poor clinical outcomes, including progressive heart failure, malignant arrhythmias, and sudden cardiac death. Content This review summarizes recent advances in artificial intelligence (AI) for the diagnosis and management of RCDs. AI technologies, including machine learning, deep learning, and multimodal data integration, enable comprehensive analysis of electrocardiography, echocardiography, cardiac magnetic resonance imaging, computed tomography, genomic and multi-omics data, biomarkers, wearable devices, and electronic health records. These approaches improve early disease detection, phenotypic classification, risk stratification, prognostic prediction and personalized treatment planning. Summary Current evidence suggests that AI significantly enhances diagnostic accuracy, prognostic assessment, and individualized clinical decision-making in patients with RCDs. Outlook Future clinical implementation requires standardized multicenter datasets, prospective validation, transparent and explainable algorithms, robust regulatory and ethical frameworks, and seamless integration into healthcare systems. Continued interdisciplinary collaboration will accelerate AI-driven precision cardiovascular medicine and improve outcomes for patients with rare cardiovascular diseases.

items.title: Cognitive engagement in a child with cerebral palsy during robot-assisted sessions: a single-case observational study
items.abstract: The aim. Children with cerebral palsy often have cognitive difficulties which make therapy more complex. Keeping their attention during structured sessions is still a challenge. However, this aspect is not widely studied in socially assistive robotics. This study aimed to describe how cognitive engagement changes across nine robot- assisted sessions in a child with cerebral palsy using the QtRobot platform. Methods. This was a single-case observational study conducted at the National Center for Children’s Rehabilitation in Astana, Kazakhstan. One 10-year-old boy with cerebral palsy participated in nine sessions. All sessions were video recorded and later analysed using behavioural mapping and a five-point Likert-type engagement scale. Each recording was divided into 10-second intervals. Engagement was evaluated based on five dimensions: verbal behaviour, non-verbal behaviour, facial expressions, gaze direction, and emotional responses. The sessions included both role-play and story-based activities, with culturally adapted Kazakh content. Results. The average engagement score across the nine sessions was 2.63 out of 5, indicating a low-to-moderate overall level of involvement. Role-play modules produced higher mean engagement (M=2.81) than story-based modules (M=2.41). Peak scores occurred at Session 1 (M=3.04) and Session 8 (M=3.00); the lowest point was Session 2 (M=2.26). After Session 1, complete disengagement was never observed. Conclusion. The findings suggest that QtRobot-assisted sessions can support and maintain cognitive engagement in a child with cerebral palsy over repeated sessions. Role-play activities appear to be more effective than story-based formats. These results support further research on robot-assisted approaches as an additional tool for cognitive and educational support in children with cerebral palsy in Kazakhstan. Keywords: cerebral palsy, cognition, rehabilitation, observational study, behavior, child.
